hints: Look carefully at the comparison: the outside solution is less negative than the inside of the cells. Which side has the higher water potential?
Remember water always moves by osmosis from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential. What happens when a plant cell gains water and pushes against its wall?
walkthrough:
**Compare the two water potentials**

Think of water potential like a hill. Water always rolls downhill.

The solution outside is less negative, so it is higher: $$\Psi_{outside} > \Psi_{inside}$$ That means the outside has the higher water potential.

**Predict the direction of osmosis**

Water moves by osmosis from higher water potential to lower water potential across the partially permeable membrane.

So here, net movement is into the cells: $$\text{water in from solution} \rightarrow \text{into cell}$$

**Link water gain to the plant cell condition**

As water enters, the vacuole and cytoplasm swell and push the cell membrane firmly against the strong cellulose cell wall.

The wall resists further expansion, so the cell becomes firm and swollen. This is called turgid, not burst and not plasmolysed.

options.A: Plant cells do not burst when they gain water because the strong cell wall provides support. Bursting only happens to animal cells with no wall.
options.B: Incipient plasmolysis is the point where water is just starting to leave and the membrane just begins to pull away. Here water is entering, not leaving.
options.C: Plasmolysed means the cell has lost water to a more negative solution outside. Here the outside is less negative, so water moves in.
options.D: Water enters by osmosis down the water potential gradient, the protoplast presses against the wall, and the cell becomes turgid.
